power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the importance of widespread, accessible viral surveillance to ensure pandemic-preparedness.
The rapid diagnosis of respiratory infections is crucial not only for effective patient management but also to inform ongoing surveillance for the detection of outbreaks.

Reverse transcriptase-Loop mediated isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP) assays are an attractive alternative to reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for rapid, decentralised testing in resource limited settings due being rapid and low cost.

Here we present the design and evaluation of a multiplexed RT-LAMP assay for the simultaneous detection of SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A and Respiratory Syncytial Virus via the incorporation of fluorescently labelled LAMP probes.
Mid-nasal swabs collected from 175 participants on the day of enrolment in the MALCOV Cohort study in Kisumu, Kenya were used in the evaluation of the RT-LAMP assay.

Overall, 114 SARS-CoV-2, six Influenza A, two Influenza B and zero RSV samples were identified in the cohort by the Allplex™ SARS-CoV-2/FluA/FluB/RSV RT-PCR kit (Seegene Inc) reference test, in addition to 53 negatives.
Sensitivity and specificity of the RT-LAMP assay (SARS-CoV-2/FluA/RSV) when compared to RT-PCR was 82.64% [CI95%:74.70-88.92%] and 100% [CI95%:93.40-100%] at 40 minutes for all samples respectively.
The mean time to a positive result was 11minutes, highlighting the speed of this technology compared to the more commonly used RT-PCR.
RT-LAMP enables rapid multi-pathogen detection with comparable diagnostic accuracy to RT-PCR.
Lower respiratory infections (LRI) and COVID-19 rank in the top ten leading causes of death globally and LRIs were the leading cause of death in low-income countries (as of 2023) (1).

text.text: Effective diagnosis and surveillance of these pathogens is crucial for effective patient management and to collect data to inform public health decision making.
The COVID-19 demonstrated the importance of pre-existing influenza surveillance systems being utilised to adapt to new threats (2, 3).

text.text: However, this came with challenges with a consultation by the World Health Organisation (WHO) found there were backlogs due to both incompatibility of equipment with new assays and resulting delays from having to perform multiple rounds of testing to establish SARS-CoV-2 status and then conduct follow up influenza screening (4).

text.text: From this consultation many countries reported that combining testing using RT-PCRs targeting multiple respiratory pathogens would be beneficial to maintain surveillance and reduce backlogs (4).

text.text: Multiplex RT-PCR is one of the primary methods for multi-pathogen detection with assays taking between 1.5-3hours to generate a result.
However, in the event of outbreaks, surveillance systems that rely on RT-PCR for sample screening can quickly become overwhelmed(4) Ref).
An alternative, faster multiplexed diagnostic method could be beneficial to reduce backlogs in such situations.
One such method is loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), a molecular assay that uses four to six primers combined with a high-strand displacement DNA polymerase (5, 6).

text.text: LAMP assays are highly target specific due to the number of regions within the genome that are targeted.

RT-LAMP (Reverse transcription -LAMP) and LAMP assays have been developed to detect a range of pathogens including, malaria, Dengue virus, Chikungunya virus, Zika virus and Hepatitis C virus all with comparable diagnostic accuracy with PCR methods (7) (8) (9) (10) (11).

text.text: In this study we set out to develop a multiplexed, probe-based RT-LAMP assay for the simultaneous detection and differentiation of SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A (H3N2) and Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSVA and RSVB).

We successfully designed and optimised a multiplex assay and evaluated its performance against a CE marked commercial RT-PCR assay on a sample set of 175 samples collected in Kisumu, Kenya throughout the pandemic from patients with respiratory symptoms.

The collection of samples and their use was reviewed and accepted by the following bodies: KEMRI Scientific and Ethics Review Unit (SERU), Kenyan Pharmacy and Poisons Board, the Health Research Ethics Committee (CERS) and Technical Committee for Clinical Trials (Comité Technique d'Examen des demandes d'autorisation Essais Cliniques
All samples were collected as part of the Malaria as a Risk Factor for COVID-19 (MALCOV) study (NCT04695197) in Western Kenya.
Mid-nasal swabs were taken from SARS-CoV-2 positive participants and stored in viral transport media (Biocomma Limited, Guangdong, China).
Samples were collected between February 2021 and February 2022.
Details of the study settings and sites involved can be found in the study protocol (22).

text.text: RT-LAMP primers were designed for three virus targets based upon sequences retrieved from GenBank representing SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A (H3N2) and Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)(A and B).

For Influenza A (H3N2) segment 7 of the Darwin 2021 strain was used as a reference for primer design (Sequence reference: OQ719010) as this was the recommended H3N2 strain for vaccine manufacturers for the 2023/2024 Influenza Season (23, 24).

text.text: We optimised one multiplex assay for simultaneous detection of four different targets (SARS-CoV-2), Influenza A (H3N2), RSVA and RSVB.
The assay can distinguish between SARS-CoV-2, influenza A (H3N2) and RSV, RSVA and B are detected in the same channel (CY5).

Primers and probes were tested on quantified controls acquired from VirCell S.L. (Granada, Spain) and ATCC (Manassas, VA, USA) representing SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A (H3N2), RSV Type A and RSV Type B and were all diluted to be used at a concentration of 1x10 3 copies/µl.

The limit of detection (LOD) was determined by conducting serial dilutions from starting stock concentrations of ~1x104 copies/µl of each target RNA and eight replicates of each dilution were performed.
Quantified viral RNA was obtained from VirCell (Granada, Spain) and ATCC (Manassas, VA, USA).

RNA from VTM of mid-nasal swabs were extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Kit (QIAGEN, Germany), following the manufacturer's protocol and implemented as an automated workflow using the QIAcube HT platform (QIAGEN, Germany).
Purified RNA was eluted in 50µl of elution buffer and stored at -80°C until use.

RNA from the 175 samples was analysed by Allplex™ SARS-CoV-2/FluA/FluB/RSV assay (SeeGene Inc, Republic of Korea) on the CFX96™ Real-time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad Inc, USA), and the RT LAMP assay.
Sensitivity and specificity of the RT-LAMP assay were calculated through comparison to the results obtained using the Allplex™ RT-PCR assay and using MedCalc for all calculations (27).

Kappa values were calculated and interpreted per variant for each assay as described in McHugh et al (28).

text.text: Here we have presented the design, validation and evaluation of a multiplex RT-LAMP assay for the differentiation of SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A and RSV (A and B).

The mean time to a positive result was 11minutes and the optimum assay time was determined to be 40 minutes; results should not be interpreted later than this in order to preserve maximum specificity and sensitivity.
While we observed the sensitivity continued to improve with time, after 40minutes the specificity begins to decrease.

Our results are in line with other multiplexed LAMP assays for SARS-CoV-2/Influenza/RSV where sensitivities range between 50.77-100% and specificities between 98.15-100% have been reported (12, 15, 16, 19, 20, 29).

text.text: Other studies used a singleplex approach in a panel to detect multiple pathogens.
One such system was able to detect ADV, Influenza A (H1N1 and H3N2), RSVA, RSVB, Influenza B and SARS-CoV-2 (12).

While this is considerably more targets than described here it would use a higher volume of sample and reagents to analyse six reactions per sample rather than a single reaction with a multiplexed assay which would improve sample throughput.
Further work should address expanding the target pathogens to include Influenza B while also investigating extraction free sample preparation methods.
LAMP has been shown to have increased tolerance to common PCR inhibitors which provides the opportunity to use LAMP on crude sample (30).
text.formatted: LAMP has been shown to have increased tolerance to common PCR inhibitors which provides the opportunity to use LAMP on crude sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(30)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, it would be beneficial to investigate using more cost-effective methods of running the assay such as the ESEQuant Tube Scanner (QIAGEN, Germany), a portable and less costly device compared to standard thermocyclers, which would allow decentralised use of the RT-LAMP assay.

To better evaluate Influenza A and RSV sensitivity, a greater number of samples should be tested, however only a limited amount of Influenza A and RSV positive samples were identified among the cohort used for this study.

To summarise, we have optimised a multiplex RT-LAMP assay capable of detecting and differentiating between SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A and RSV viruses and have demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity when compared to a commercial RT-PCR assay.
This assay would be beneficial for outbreak scenarios to alleviate backlogs of sample testing due to its combination of a short run time, multiplex target identification, and sensitivity, .
It can be used on modern thermocyclers so can easily be incorporated into existing testing workflows in laboratories with a qPCR machine.
